title: CPU Caches & The Memory Hierarchy
tagline: Why a cache miss costs ~100x an L1 hit — and how data layout, not clever code, wins the latency game.

concept.analogy: Think of the CPU as a chef and memory as a giant warehouse across town. The chef's hands (registers) hold what's being used right now. The countertop (L1) holds the current recipe's ingredients. A nearby pantry (L2) and the kitchen's walk-in fridge (L3) hold a bit more. DRAM is the warehouse — a round trip there stalls the chef for what feels like forever. A good chef arranges ingredients so almost everything needed is already on the counter; a bad one runs to the warehouse for every single item.
paragraphs: Modern CPUs are fast; main memory is comparatively glacial. A single DRAM access can cost ~60–100 nanoseconds, during which a 3 GHz core could have executed hundreds of instructions. To hide this, the hardware keeps a hierarchy of caches: L1 (per-core, ~32 KB, ~1 ns / ~4 cycles), L2 (per-core, ~256 KB–1 MB, ~4 ns), and L3 (shared, several MB to tens of MB, ~10–20 ns). The further out you go, the bigger and slower.

Caches move data in fixed-size blocks called cache lines — almost always 64 bytes. Touch one byte and the whole 64-byte line is pulled in. This is why spatial locality (using bytes near each other) and temporal locality (reusing bytes soon) are the two levers that decide real-world performance. The hardware prefetcher also watches your access pattern and speculatively pulls in lines ahead of a sequential stream.

For HFT, the headline fact is the cliff: an L1 hit is roughly 1 ns, an L3 hit ~15 ns, and a miss to DRAM ~80–100 ns. A hot loop that misses cache on every iteration can be 50–100x slower than the same loop hitting L1 — even though the C++ source looks identical. The instruction stream also lives in caches (I-cache), so bloated, branchy code can stall on instruction-cache misses too.

The practical takeaway is counterintuitive for newcomers: on the hot path, how your data is laid out in memory usually matters more than the cleverness of your algorithm. Compact, contiguous, sequentially-accessed data that fits in cache beats a 'smarter' structure that chases pointers all over the heap.
points: Caches move 64-byte lines; touching one byte loads its whole line.
Rough latencies: register ~0, L1 ~1 ns, L2 ~4 ns, L3 ~15 ns, DRAM ~80–100 ns.
Spatial + temporal locality are the two levers; the hardware prefetcher rewards sequential access.
On the hot path, data layout often beats algorithmic cleverness.
Code also lives in cache — bloated/branchy hot paths suffer I-cache misses.

callouts.title: Structure of Arrays (SoA)
callouts.body: If a loop only reads the `price` field of a million orders, store all prices contiguously (SoA) rather than as a field inside a fat struct (AoS). You then load only useful bytes per cache line instead of dragging along fields you don't touch.

callouts.title: Pointer chasing kills throughput
callouts.body: Linked lists, node-based maps, and `shared_ptr` graphs scatter data across the heap. Each `next` is a likely cache miss the prefetcher can't predict. Prefer flat arrays / open-addressing hash maps on the hot path.

concept.keyIdea: Memory is a hierarchy and the unit of transfer is the 64-byte cache line. Make hot data compact, contiguous, and accessed sequentially so it stays in L1/L2 — because a cache miss to DRAM can cost 50–100x an L1 hit, dwarfing most algorithmic savings.

deepDive.intro: How the hierarchy works, why sequential beats random by an order of magnitude, and the layout patterns that exploit it.

steps.title: Lines, sets, and associativity
steps.detail: A cache is organized into sets of N 'ways' (e.g. 8-way associative). An address maps to one set; any of its N lines can hold that data. When a set is full, a line is evicted (roughly LRU). Two hot addresses that map to the same set can repeatedly evict each other ('conflict misses') even when the cache is mostly empty — a subtle cause of slowdowns with power-of-two strides.

steps.title: The hardware prefetcher
steps.detail: When you stream through memory sequentially (or with a fixed stride), the prefetcher detects the pattern and fetches upcoming lines before you ask. This is why iterating a contiguous array is dramatically faster than the same number of random accesses: the misses are hidden. Random / pointer-chasing patterns defeat the prefetcher, so every access pays full DRAM latency.

steps.title: AoS vs SoA
steps.detail: Array-of-Structs (`struct Order{double px; int qty; char sym[8]; ...}; Order arr[N];`) is natural but wasteful when a loop touches one field: each 64-byte line is mostly the fields you ignore. Struct-of-Arrays keeps each field in its own contiguous array, so a price-only scan loads ~8 prices per line instead of 1. SoA is a cornerstone of data-oriented design.

steps.title: Working set and capacity
steps.detail: If your hot working set fits in L1/L2, you stay fast; once it spills to L3 or DRAM, latency jumps. Keep per-event state small, reuse buffers, and prefer fixed-capacity containers. A 1 MB lookup table that thrashes L2 can be slower than recomputing a value that stays in registers.

steps.title: Measuring it
steps.detail: Use `perf stat -e cache-misses,L1-dcache-load-misses,LLC-load-misses ./app` to see miss rates, and `perf record`/`perf report` to find the offending lines. Don't guess — cache behavior is unintuitive, and the bottleneck is rarely where you think.

notes.title: Alignment helps but is not magic
notes.detail: Aligning hot structures to cache-line boundaries avoids straddling two lines, but the bigger win is touching fewer lines overall. Compactness first, alignment second.

notes.title: Latency vs bandwidth
notes.detail: Sequential access is fast partly because DRAM delivers high bandwidth in bursts; the cost you fight on random access is latency, which prefetching and pipelining cannot hide.

complexity.timeReason: Big-O counts operations, not memory stalls. Two O(n) loops can differ 10–100x because one is L1-resident and the other misses to DRAM every iteration.
complexity.spaceReason: A working set that fits in L1/L2 stays fast; spilling to DRAM is the cliff. Compact representations are a performance feature, not just a memory saving.

pitfalls: Reasoning about hot-path speed purely from Big-O while ignoring the memory hierarchy.
Node-based containers (std::list, std::map, pointer graphs) on the hot path — every hop is a likely miss.
Fat structs scanned for one field (use SoA), and power-of-two strides causing conflict misses.
Trusting intuition instead of `perf` — the real bottleneck is usually a surprise.

benchmark.takeaway: An L1 hit vs a DRAM miss is roughly 1 ns vs 80 ns — an 80x gap created entirely by where the data lives. Winning latency is mostly about keeping hot data in cache, not shaving instructions.

interviewQuestions.q: What is a cache line, how big is it, and why does its size matter for performance?
a: A cache line is the fixed-size block the CPU transfers between memory and cache — almost always 64 bytes on x86/ARM server cores. The cache never moves single bytes; touching one byte loads its entire 64-byte line.

It matters because it sets the granularity of locality: sequential access reuses already-loaded lines and triggers the prefetcher (cheap), while scattered access pays a full miss per line (expensive). It also explains false sharing (two threads hammering different variables that happen to share a line), and why packing hot fields together and unrelated-but-contended fields apart both help.

interviewQuestions.q: Two nested loops sum a large 2D matrix; one is row-major, one column-major. Same operations and Big-O. Why is one much slower, and by how much?
a: Row-major iteration walks memory with stride 1, so each 64-byte line yields ~16 ints and the hardware prefetcher streams the next lines — almost everything is an L1/L2 hit. Column-major iteration walks with stride = row length, touching a new (cold) line on nearly every access, so it misses to DRAM repeatedly and defeats the prefetcher.

The slowdown is typically 5–10x (sometimes more for large matrices), driven purely by cache-miss latency, not instruction count. It's the canonical demonstration that the memory access pattern, not Big-O, decides hot-loop performance.

interviewQuestions.q: You suspect a hot loop is memory-bound. How do you confirm it and find the culprit?
a: Measure, don't guess. Use `perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-references,cache-misses,L1-dcache-load-misses,LLC-load-misses ./app` to see the miss rates and IPC (instructions-per-cycle) — low IPC with high LLC miss rate signals memory-bound.

Then `perf record` / `perf report` (and tools like VTune or `toplev`) to attribute misses to specific lines. Confirm by changing the data layout (e.g., SoA, smaller structs, contiguous storage) and re-measuring: if latency tracks the miss rate, it was the memory hierarchy.

problems.title: Refactor AoS to SoA and predict the win
problems.statement: Given `struct Tick{ double px; int64_t qty; char sym[8]; uint32_t flags; };` and a vector of 10 million ticks, a hot loop computes the max `px`. Refactor to SoA, and explain quantitatively (in terms of bytes per cache line) why the SoA version should be faster. Roughly what speedup would you expect on the price-only scan?
problems.hint: Count how many useful prices fit in one 64-byte line under AoS vs SoA.

approach: Under AoS, each Tick is 8 + 8 + 8 + 4 = 28 bytes (padded to 32). A 64-byte line holds ~2 Ticks, so a price-only scan brings in ~2 useful 8-byte prices and ~48 bytes of qty/sym/flags you never read — about 25% useful bandwidth.

Under SoA, `std::vector<double> px` is dense: one 64-byte line holds 8 prices, all useful — 100% useful bandwidth, and the prefetcher streams it perfectly. So you fetch ~4x fewer lines for the same scan.

Expect roughly a 3–4x speedup on the price-only scan (bounded by the bandwidth ratio), more if the AoS struct were larger. The exact number depends on whether the data was already cache-resident, so always measure with perf.

problems.title: Diagnose a power-of-two slowdown
problems.statement: A colleague reports that processing a 1024x1024 float matrix column-wise is far slower than a 1023x1023 one, despite being nearly the same size. Explain what's happening and how you'd fix it without changing the algorithm.
problems.hint: Think about cache associativity and which set each column element maps to.

approach: With a 1024-wide row, the stride between vertically-adjacent elements is exactly a power of two (1024 floats = 4096 bytes). Such strides map many elements to the same cache set, so an N-way cache evicts useful lines repeatedly — classic conflict misses — even though total data is small. The 1023 width breaks the alignment, spreading accesses across sets.

Fixes that keep the algorithm: pad each row (e.g., allocate width 1024+8) so the stride is no longer a power of two; or block/tile the traversal so you reuse lines within a small sub-block before moving on; or transpose once if you'll scan columns repeatedly. Each restores set diversity or restores stride-1 locality.
Confirm with `perf stat` — you should see the high cache-miss / low-IPC profile collapse after padding or tiling.
